 Author(s) 
 Tsegaye T. Gatiso 
 Mei Sun Yee 
 Counting the hidden costs of natural hazards: Understanding post-flood demand surge in the construction sector in New Zealand
 Source 
 Economics of Disasters and Climate Change (Springer) 
 Upload your content 
 This study addresses this gap by examining the impact of two quick-succession flood events in 2023 (Auckland Anniversary floods and Cyclone Gabrielle) on Auckland’s construction sector. Using geographic unit-level data from the Statistics New Zealand Longitudinal Business Database, we analyse the impact of the flood events on labour demand, wages, and construction material costs. To strengthen causal inference, we combine propensity score matching with an event study framework.
 The results revealed a significant demand surge in Auckland, particularly in the residential building sector. In Auckland, labour costs increased by 24% in 2024 relative to the control regions and pre-flood events. This increase was driven by both an increase in employment (8%) and wages per worker (16%). Auckland’s construction services sector also experienced an increase in labour costs (13%), employment (6%) and wage per worker (9%). In contrast, changes in construction material costs were statistically insignificant across all the construction subsectors. Moreover, the researchers found no significant demand surge in the non-residential building or heavy engineering sectors both in terms of cost of labour and construction materials. The findings demonstrate that the demand surge effects of the 2023 flood events in Auckland were highly construction sector-specific and primarily driven by labour market pressures.
